Effect Fidelity Report Card

How much to trust the wrong-call number

A call is one of three answers: ship B, keep A, or no clear difference, read from a 95% interval. It is 'wrong' if it differs from the call the full real study supports. Of the 17 experiments, the full real data says B is better in 10, A in 3, and no clear difference in 4. Trivial strategies score: always 'ship B' 41% wrong, always 'no difference' 76%, a random pick of the three 67%, a coin flip between A and B 62%. So with 17 experiments the wrong-call rate alone separates simulators poorly; always shipping B beats every simulator here. A simulator's call also depends on how many simulated people were run (more people, narrower interval), so the table below scores every simulator at the same 25 simulated people per arm and adds two measures that don't depend on that number.

When is a simulated A/B result good enough to trust? A benchmark of LLM persona simulators against 17 real randomized experiments with public ground truth.

Headline. Per-question accuracy does not guarantee effect accuracy. Across the 5 simulators, 23 simulated experiments had both arms within TVD 0.15 of the real answer distributions, yet 13 of those still led to the wrong ship/no-ship call (e.g. Hillstrom women's email, blind prompt: both arms within TVD 0.15, simulated lift 15.3 pp vs. real 4.5 pp; GSS 'assistance to Black people' wording, Llama: both arms within TVD 0.11, simulated +1.3 pp vs. real -6.7 pp). For the simulator with the best per-arm accuracy (Claude Opus 5.5, real-respondent personas, mean arm TVD 0.15), the calibration slope of simulated on real effects was 1.06 (1.0 = right size), its 95% intervals covered the real effect in 76% of 17 experiments, and a held-out recalibration raised coverage to 94%. The small open models shrank effects toward zero (slopes 0.06-0.42); Claude got the size about right (slopes 1.03-1.06) but was still often wrong about direction or significance. Effect-level checks complement distribution-level ones.

"Ratio" and "sign" use only experiments whose real 95% CI excludes zero (13 of 17); the other 4 are real nulls, which test whether a simulator invents effects. A "call" is what a team would do from that result: ship B, keep A, or no detectable difference (95% CI includes 0).

Per-arm accuracy vs. effect accuracy

Distribution-level metrics, like total variation distance (TVD) between simulated and real answer distributions for a single question, are the natural way to score a population simulation, and Simile's confidence model reports exactly this kind of quantity. A decision, though, usually depends on the difference between two arms. Two arms can each be close to reality while their errors don't cancel, so the gap between them is wrong. This section measures both on the same runs. TVD is computed per arm on answers rounded to the nearest scale point; 0.15 is used as a reference line because it has been reported (unverified, secondhand) as a "decision-ready" bar.

Experiments with both arms under TVD 0.15, per simulator: {"Qwen2.5-1.5B, blind prompt": 3, "Qwen2.5-1.5B, real-respondent personas": 3, "Llama-3.2-1B, real-respondent personas": 1, "Claude Opus 5.5, blind prompt": 8, "Claude Opus 5.5, real-respondent personas": 8}. Wrong-call rate among them: {"Qwen2.5-1.5B, blind prompt": 0.33, "Qwen2.5-1.5B, real-respondent personas": 0.67, "Llama-3.2-1B, real-respondent personas": 1.0, "Claude Opus 5.5, blind prompt": 0.38, "Claude Opus 5.5, real-respondent personas": 0.75}. Correlation between worse-arm TVD and effect error: {"Qwen2.5-1.5B, blind prompt": 0.46, "Qwen2.5-1.5B, real-respondent personas": 0.34, "Llama-3.2-1B, real-respondent personas": 0.02, "Claude Opus 5.5, blind prompt": 0.6, "Claude Opus 5.5, real-respondent personas": 0.15}. The recommendation is to add both: per-arm distribution accuracy plus an effect-level fidelity check for experiment-style questions.

Does the simulator get the size right?

Each point is one experiment, in units of the real respondents' standard deviation so different outcomes are comparable. Points on the dashed line would be perfect. Error bars are the simulator's own bootstrap 95% CI.

Every experiment

Can a simple correction fix it?

For each experiment, the correction is fit only on the other 16 experiments (leave-one-experiment-out): a single scale factor (real ≈ c × simulated, in SD units) plus a "model error" variance τ², which is the spread of real effects around the rescaled simulation that sampling noise cannot explain. The corrected 95% interval is c×sim ± 1.96√(c²se² + τ²). The point: a simulator's own bootstrap interval only captures sampling noise, which more draws shrink toward zero; the dominant uncertainty is model error, and it has to be estimated against real experiments.

How many real people do you still need?

Instead of replacing real respondents, can a simulator stretch a small real sample? We tested the standard way to do that safely.

Take a small batch of real people (25 to 500 per version). Ask the simulator to predict each of those same people's answers from their own background (age, politics, purchase history…) without seeing what they actually said. Also ask it about a larger group of people whose answers we pretend not to know. Where the simulator's guesses for the real batch miss, we measure by how much and use that to correct its guesses for the larger group. If the simulator is useless, the method notices and quietly falls back to the real data alone, so the answer can't get worse than real-only (up to noise); if it's good, the uncertainty range shrinks. This is prediction-powered inference (PPI++, Angelopoulos et al. 2023), the same idea as the mixed subjects design of Broska, Howes & van Loon (2025).

The simulator is worth essentially zero extra real respondents: median worth at 100 real people per arm is Llama-3.2-1B, real-respondent personas 1.00x, Qwen2.5-1.5B, real-respondent personas 1.00x, and the wrong-call rate with real + simulator is the same as with real people alone at every sample size. Claude Opus 5.5, real-respondent personas was only tested with 25 real people per arm (a quick run with a small real pool); there it was worth 1.03x, also about nothing. The reason is simple: a model's guess for a person barely tracks what that person actually answered (median correlation Claude Opus 5.5, real-respondent personas 0.14, Llama-3.2-1B, real-respondent personas -0.01, Qwen2.5-1.5B, real-respondent personas -0.00). PPI did its job, though: it noticed the simulator was uninformative, gave it almost no weight, and kept the uncertainty range honest. The curve is the yardstick a better simulator has to beat.

For each of the 17 experiments with person-level predictions, each persona simulator and each sample size, we drew 500 random real samples and compared three ways of estimating the effect against the answer from the full real study: real people only, simulator only, and real + simulator (PPI). "Worth" is the effective sample size: how many real people you'd need, with real data only, to get an equally narrow range, divided by how many you actually used.

With a large unlabeled group, the worth is about 1 / (1 − r²), where r is the correlation between the simulator's prediction for a person and that person's real answer. Doubling your sample needs r ≈ 0.71; a 25% boost needs r ≈ 0.45. Median r here: Claude Opus 5.5, real-respondent personas 0.14 (max 0.62), Llama-3.2-1B, real-respondent personas -0.01 (max 0.26), Qwen2.5-1.5B, real-respondent personas -0.00 (max 0.15).

Design choices and assumptions

  • The original simulation runs used random personas, not linked to specific real people, which PPI can't use. So we re-ran each persona simulator on the real respondents' own covariates (covariate-matched pairing). Because the prediction only uses pre-treatment covariates and never the outcome, PPI's guarantee holds no matter how biased the simulator is.
  • A random 1,000 real respondents per arm for the first six Many Labs experiments and 600 for the rest (cut to fit CPU time; Hillstrom's full 21k per arm would take days on a laptop CPU). n is capped at half the pool, so 500 becomes 300 where the pool is 600. The n "labeled" people are drawn from that pool and the rest act as the unlabeled group, so the unlabeled group is at most ~40x the labeled one. Real deployments with a big panel would gain a bit more.
  • The simulator's probability-weighted (expected) answer. For the multi-item flag, money and contact scales the prediction uses the first 2 items as a short form, to save compute; the real outcome is still the full scale.
  • Blind prompts give everyone the same prediction, so they carry no person-level information and PPI gives them exactly zero weight. They're excluded here.
  • Truth is the full real study's effect (all respondents), and "wrong call" compares (ship B / keep A / no clear difference) from a 95% interval against that full-study call. At small n, real-only is often "wrong" simply because it can't yet see a real effect.
  • Li & Ji (2026, arXiv 2604.02458) already showed that realistic-looking simulated answers don't imply correct effects; Broska et al. (2025) proposed combining simulated and real subjects with PPI. What's added here is the measurement on 17 public experiments, at the level of decisions, with small open models, reproducible end to end.

Method

  • Computed here from respondent-level public microdata (no hand-entered numbers): difference in means with a 95% bootstrap CI. Binary outcomes are in percentage points, rating scales in scale points.
  • Local open-weight models via llama.cpp (4-bit GGUF, CPU). Each simulated respondent sees the original question wording for its arm. The model's next-token probabilities over the answer options give an answer distribution, and one answer is sampled per respondent. "Blind" = one generic respondent description; "persona" = each simulated respondent is built from a real respondent drawn from the same study (age, sex, and political identity for Many Labs; age, sex, race, education and political views for GSS; purchase history, channel and location for the email RCT). 25 simulated respondents per arm; bootstrap CIs (2,000 resamples) over simulated respondents. Multi-item scales are averaged like the original.
  • Priming manipulations (flag, money, imagined contact) are visual or experiential in the original; here they are described in text. That is a known limitation of text-only simulation, and it is what a vendor would face too.
  • Every simulator run is logged to MLflow (local file store, mlruns/) with parameters, all metrics and per-experiment tables. New model calls this run: {"qwen15_blind": 69, "qwen15_persona": 7360, "llama32_1b_persona": 7357, "claude_blind": 69, "claude_persona": 1637}; responses are cached in data/cache/.

Caveats

  • The simulators are small (1–1.5B-parameter) open-weight models running on a CPU, chosen because no hosted-model API keys were available. Frontier models or a purpose-built behavior model will score differently; the harness is model-agnostic and the point is the measurement.
  • 17 experiments is a small benchmark, and the correction has 16 training points per fold. Treat the recalibration as a demonstration of the method, not a production calibrator.
  • Many Labs 1 participants are mostly US undergraduates and MTurk workers; GSS effects are unweighted; the email RCT measures site visits within two weeks.
  • Many of these effects are famous and appear in model training data, which should make them easier for a simulator, not harder.
